propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 26, 2021 decision refusing permanent residence on H&C grounds
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Sathiyarajah Amarasingam, seeks judicial review, pursuant to section 72 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], of a decision dated May 26, 2021, of a Senior Immigration Officer [the Officer] refusing the Applicant’s application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds.

propositions.text: Applicant argues the decision is unreasonable
propositions.quote: On judicial review, the Applicant argues that the decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 26, 2021 refusal of permanent residence on H&C grounds and argues the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed and matter remitted to different officer for reconsideration
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, the application for judicial review is allowed. The matter is remitted to a different immigration officer for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review and remits matter to different officer for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Applicant is 52-year-old Sri Lankan citizen who entered Canada in 2011 and claimed refugee status as Tamil Hindu minority member
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 52-year-old citizen of Sri Lanka. He entered Canada on January 7, 2011, and made a refugee claim on the basis that he was being persecuted as a member of a minority community in Sri Lanka, the Tamil Hindu.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is a 52-year-old Sri Lankan citizen who entered Canada in 2011 and claimed refugee status as Tamil Hindu minority member.

propositions.text: Applicant was detained and persecuted during Sri Lankan civil war and faced harassment in government-controlled territory
propositions.quote: As a youth and young man, during the civil war in Sri Lanka, the Applicant was allegedly detained and exposed to various persecutions. He and his family left the part of the country that was controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam [LTTE], a militant secessionist organization, and began living in the government-controlled territory. There, he continued to face harassment, mob attacks, extortion, and robbery, on the suspicion that he was associated with the LTTE.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges detention and persecution during civil war and harassment in government-controlled territory in Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Refused refugee claim in 2012 as attacks were criminal and risks generalized
propositions.quote: On March 26, 2012, his refugee claim was refused on the basis that the motivation for the attacks and extortion were criminal in nature and that the threat of future extortion or kidnapping was a generalized risk faced by others in the country.

propositions.text: Judicial review leave of refugee claim refusal denied August 15, 2012
propositions.quote: He sought leave for judicial review of the decision, but his application was denied on August 15, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker refused refugee claim in 2012 as attacks were criminal and risks generalized; judicial review leave denied.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for permanent residence on H&C grounds June 2012, refused June 2013
propositions.quote: On June 21, 2012, he submitted an application for permanent residence on H&C grounds, which was also refused on June 24, 2013.

propositions.text: Removal order issued December 23, 2012; Applicant did not appear due to fear of return
propositions.quote: An order for removal was issued against him to leave Canada on December 23, 2012. The Applicant did not appear for his removal because of his alleged continued fear to return to Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found Applicant applied for permanent residence on H&C grounds in 2012, refused in 2013; removal order issued but Applicant did not appear due to fear.

propositions.text: Warrant issued December 27, 2012; Applicant remained and worked without authorization until warrant executed August 20, 2020
propositions.quote: On December 27, 2012, a warrant was issued against him. However, he continued to remain and work in Canada without authorization for an extended period of time. The warrant against him was executed on August 20, 2020, and he was released with conditions.

paragraphs.summary: Warrant issued December 2012; Applicant remained and worked without authorization until warrant executed August 2020.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted second permanent residence application on H&C grounds August 19, 2020 citing establishment, children's best interests, and adverse country conditions
propositions.quote: Upon the execution of the warrant, on August 19, 2020, the Applicant submitted a second application for permanent residence based on H&C grounds. The motives for this application were his level of establishment in Canada, the best interest of the children, and the adverse country conditions in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted second permanent residence application on H&C grounds in August 2020 citing establishment, children's best interests, and adverse country conditions.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application March 16, 2021
propositions.quote: On March 16, 2021, he submitted a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment [PRRA] application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application in March 2021.

propositions.text: H&C application and PRRA refused May 26, 2021; Officer not satisfied humanitarian and compassionate considerations justified exemption under IRPA s 25(1)
propositions.quote: After conducting a global assessment of all the factors raised by the Applicant, the H&C application was denied on May 26, 2021. The Applicant’s PRRA decision was also refused at the same time by the same Officer. The Officer was not satisfied that the humanitarian and compassionate considerations justified an exemption under subsection 25(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker refused H&C application and PRRA in May 2021, not satisfied humanitarian and compassionate considerations justified exemption under IRPA s 25(1).

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant had some establishment but noted prolonged unauthorized presence and failure to appear for removal in 2012
propositions.quote: With regards to the criterion of establishment, the Officer concluded that the Applicant had a degree of establishment in Canada. Nevertheless, the Officer also noted that the Applicant continued to remain and work in Canada without authorization for a prolonged period. The Officer also considered that the Applicant had failed to appear for removal on December 23, 2012, and had subsequently gone underground for more than eight years.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant had some establishment but prolonged unauthorized presence and failure to appear for removal in 2012.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant showed disregard for Canadian regulations by not regularizing status until recently, negatively affecting application
propositions.quote: Because the Applicant did not make further attempts to regularize his status in Canada during that period, until recently, the Officer found that the Applicant had shown disregard for Canadian regulations and that this failure negatively affected his application.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant showed disregard for Canadian regulations by not regularizing status until recently, negatively affecting application.

propositions.text: Officer found insufficient evidence that Applicant would be discriminated or mistreated as Tamil returnee or long-term resident
propositions.quote: With regards to the risks and adverse country conditions, the Officer concluded that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Applicant would, on a balance of probabilities, be discriminated against or mistreated simply as a result of his status as a Tamil returnee and also as a person who had resided in Canada for the past decade.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found insufficient evidence Applicant would be discriminated or mistreated as Tamil returnee or long-term resident.

propositions.text: Officer found insufficient corroborative evidence of past mistreatment by army or paramilitary and no evidence of ongoing threat in Sri Lanka
propositions.quote: More specifically regarding the forward-looking hardships that the Applicant would face upon his return to Sri Lanka, the Officer found that the Applicant did not provide sufficient corroborative evidence of past mistreatment or abuse at the hands of the army or People’s Liberation Organisation of Tamil Eelam, a pro-government paramilitary group supporting the LTTE. The Officer further noted that the Applicant resided in Canada for over ten years and had not objectively established with sufficient evidence that anyone in Sri Lanka had an ongoing interest to locate and harm him.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found insufficient evidence of past mistreatment or ongoing threat in Sri Lanka upon return.

propositions.text: Officer relied on evidence that detention targets have significant political activity, which Applicant did not establish
propositions.quote: The Officer also relied on documentary evidence indicating that those who are likely to be detained and interrogated upon return are individuals with a history of significant political activity, which the Applicant had not established. The Officer found that the Applicant had presented insufficient evidence to demonstrate that anyone in Sri Lanka perceives or would perceive him to be related to the LTTE supporter or sympathizers.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant did not establish political activity or perception of LTTE association to justify detention risk.

propositions.text: Officer noted discrimination against Tamils exists but Applicant did not show hardship level justifying exemption
propositions.quote: The Officer also noted that while discrimination against Tamils is clearly present in Sri Lanka, the Applicant had not demonstrated that he would face a level of hardship that would justify an exemption from legislative requirements (H&C considerations). In fact, the Officer noted that insufficient evidence had been provided to show that the Applicant’s family members who still reside in Visuvamadu in the Northern Province of Sri Lanka were denied access to education, employment, health services, or other social services.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted Tamil discrimination but found Applicant did not show hardship level justifying exemption.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant resilient, able to adapt on return with family support and transferable skills
propositions.quote: The Officer further found that the Applicant is a resilient individual who will be able to adapt upon his return to Sri Lanka as his family members will be able to support him financially. The skills he obtained as an assembler, general labourer, and maintenance worker in Canada will also be transferrable for him in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant resilient and able to adapt on return with family support and transferable skills.

propositions.text: Determinative issue is whether Officer’s refusal of H&C application was reasonable
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this judicial review is whether the Officer’s decision to refuse the H&C application was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court states determinative issue is whether Officer’s refusal of H&C application was reasonable.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness as set out in Vavilov 2019 SCC 65
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review is one of reasonableness as set out in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]. A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review is reasonableness as set out in Vavilov 2019 SCC 65.

propositions.text: Court may intervene if decision has serious shortcomings beyond superficial or peripheral flaws
propositions.quote: For the reviewing court to intervene, the challenging party must satisfy the court that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency”, and that such alleged shortcomings or flaws are “more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: Court may intervene if decision has serious shortcomings beyond superficial or peripheral flaws, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: The decision ignores relevant evidence and applies illogical reasoning, making it neither justifiable nor intelligible.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that because the decision ignores relevant evidence and applies illogical reasoning, it is neither justifiable nor intelligible (Vavilov at paras 104, 126).

propositions.text: Reasonableness may be jeopardized if decision maker misapprehended or failed to account for evidence, or if reasons show clear logical fallacies.
propositions.quote: the reasonableness of a decision may be jeopardized where the decision maker has fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it” and “the internal rationality of a decision may be called into question if the reasons exhibit clear logical fallacies

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues decision ignores evidence and is illogical; Vavilov says reasonableness is jeopardized by ignoring evidence or logical fallacies.

propositions.text: Decision maker cannot selectively choose evidence and ignore contradicting facts; must consider and weigh all evidence and explain contrary evidence.
propositions.quote: a decision maker cannot selectively choose evidence and ignore contradicting facts. Instead, the decision maker must demonstrate that all of the evidence was considered and weighed

propositions.text: Intervening is appropriate when decision maker did not properly mention contradicting facts and court cannot assess meaningful consideration of key issues.
propositions.quote: intervening because the decision maker did not properly mention contradicting facts is appropriate when the Court cannot assess whether the decision maker meaningfully considered all of the key issues and evidence

propositions.text: Overturning a decision for not discussing critical contradicting evidence is not disguised correctness but shows failure to consider relevant evidence or argument.
propositions.quote: Overturning a decision because the reasons did not discuss critical contradicting evidence is not “disguised correctness” - nor the application of a court established “yardstick” to measure the decision maker’s reasons

paragraphs.summary: Court explains decision makers must consider all evidence and explain contrary evidence; failure to do so justifies intervention.

propositions.text: Officer turned positive H&C factors into negative ones, contrary to jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the Decision is unreasonable because the Officer turned positive H&C factors into negative ones, contrary to the rule established by jurisprudence.

propositions.text: Officer used Applicant's resilience to justify conclusion he could adapt to home country, which is unreasonable per Singh.
propositions.quote: despite noting the discrimination the Applicant might face, the Officer points to his resilience as a way to justify his conclusion that “he will be able to adapt to the environment of his home country after an initial period of adjustment.” In Singh v Canada

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer unreasonably turned positive factors negative, citing Singh case.

propositions.text: Officer ignored relevant evidence contradicting decision that Applicant was unable to demonstrate risk if removed after over ten years.
propositions.quote: the Officer ignored relevant evidence that contradicted their decision that the Applicant was unable to demonstrate a risk if removed, on a balance of probabilities and more than ten years after having left Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer ignored relevant contradictory evidence about risk after removal.

propositions.text: Same Officer decided PRRA and H&C applications on same record but excluded relevant PRRA analysis from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: the Officer deciding the H&C application in this case was the same Officer that was also considering the PRRA application, and both decisions rested on the exact same record. However, despite copying the PRRA analysis into the H&C decision, the Officer excluded the sections of the PRRA analysis that were in fact more relevant to an H&C analysis.

propositions.text: PRRA analysis cited sources showing increased military presence and harassment of Tamils, but these were absent from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: in the PRRA analysis (but absent from consideration in the H&C decision), the decision maker cited a source from Freedom House in 2019 indicating that military presence increased in Tamil-populated areas and that the government encouraged settlement with the aim of diluting local Tamil majorities. The decision maker also cited a US Department of State Report of 2020 in which Tamils are reporting events of harassment at the hands of security forces.

propositions.text: PRRA analysis concluded human rights abuses against Tamils may still not be fully addressed and discrimination continues.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence I have consulted demonstrates that human rights abuses committed in the past in Sri Lanka may still not have been fully addressed by the government. Tamils may continue to face discrimination due to their ethnicity.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes Officer excluded relevant PRRA evidence of military presence and discrimination from H&C decision.

propositions.text: Officer either did not appreciate differences between PRRA and H&C tests or improperly excluded positive information from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the Officer either did not properly appreciate the differences between the PRRA and H&C tests, or simply improperly excluded information from the H&C decision that should have been given positive weight.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer misunderstood PRRA vs H&C or improperly excluded positive evidence in H&C decision.

propositions.text: Officer gave no weight to evidence of discrimination against Tamils, repeated PRRA risk analysis, and applied wrong legal requirements for H&C test.
propositions.quote: the Officer gave no weight to the available evidence of discrimination against Tamils, opting instead to repeat the risk analysis of the PRRA. In doing so, the Officer applied the same legal requirements, despite the fact that the criteria are different for the H&C test.

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider relevant factors through humanitarian and compassionate lens, dismissing discrimination and adverse country conditions.
propositions.quote: the Officer failed to consider relevant factors through a humanitarian and compassionate lens. Overall, by applying the more onerous PRRA standards and dismissing relevant evidence of discrimination, militarization, and adverse country conditions

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits Officer wrongly applied PRRA standards and ignored relevant H&C factors like discrimination and adverse conditions.

propositions.text: Officer considered whether discrimination amounted to hardship justifying positive H&C, finding insufficient evidence of family hardship or support.
propositions.quote: the Officer turned their mind to whether the level of discrimination faced by the Applicant amounted to a hardship that justified a positive H&C, finding that there was insufficient evidence that his family in Sri Lanka was facing difficulties and that they could help him settle upon his return.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says Officer considered discrimination as hardship and found insufficient evidence of family hardship or support.

propositions.text: Officer's overall assessment was reasonable based on evidence before them, including discrimination against similarly situated individuals.
propositions.quote: The Officer considered the evidence of discrimination against similarly situated individuals, such as the Applicant’s family in Sri Lanka, and found that it did not amount to hardship.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably assessed current situation of Applicant’s family and found no hardship warranting H&C relief.
propositions.quote: it was open to the Officer to look at what the current situation for the Applicant’s family was at the time of evaluation, and find that it didn’t rise to the level where H&C relief was warranted.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer reasonably assessed family situation and found no hardship warranting H&C relief.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably considered Applicant’s establishment factors independently and gave negative weight in context of immigration history.
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably considered the Applicant’s establishment factors independently from the assessment of the hardship in Sri Lanka and gave it negative weight within the context of his whole immigration history.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits Officer reasonably gave negative weight to establishment factors in context of immigration history.

propositions.text: Subsection 25(1) IRPA gives Minister discretion to grant permanent resident status for humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA provides the Minister with the discretionary power to exempt a foreigner from having to meet any criteria or obligation of the IRPA and to grant him/her permanent resident status, if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

propositions.text: Section 25(1) IRPA text is provided, outlining Minister's discretion and conditions for H&C relief.
propositions.quote: Humanitarian and compassionate considerations — request of foreign national Séjour pour motif d’ordre humanitaire à la demande de l’étranger 25 (1) Subject to subsection (1.2), the Minister must, on request of a foreign national in Canada who applies for permanent resident status and who is inadmissible

paragraphs.summary: Court states s.25(1) IRPA grants Minister discretion to grant permanent residence for humanitarian and compassionate reasons.

propositions.text: Applicants bear onus to satisfy decision maker that H&C relief is justified under IRPA.
propositions.quote: applicants who apply for H&C considerations bear the onus of satisfying the decision maker that the granting of permanent resident status or an exemption from any applicable criteria or obligations of the IRPA is justified by H&C considerations

paragraphs.summary: Court states applicants bear onus to prove H&C relief is justified.

propositions.text: Test for H&C relief requires showing misfortunes that excite desire to relieve them, beyond ordinary hardship of removal.
propositions.quote: Section 25 of the IRPA provides exceptional relief from what would otherwise be the ordinary operation of the IRPA. To obtain such relief, an applicant bears the onus of establishing circumstances that “would excite in a reasonable [person] in a civilized community a desire to relieve the misfortunes of another”

propositions.text: Applicants must show misfortunes or circumstances exceptional relative to others applying for permanent residence.
propositions.quote: applicants for H&C relief must demonstrate the existence or likely existence of misfortunes or other H&C considerations that are greater than those typically faced by others who apply for permanent residence in Canada.

propositions.text: All relevant facts and factors advanced by applicant must be considered and weighed in H&C discretion.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether an applicant has established sufficient H&C considerations to warrant a favourable exercise of discretion under s. 25 of the IRPA, all of the relevant facts and factors advanced by the applicant must be considered and weighed

paragraphs.summary: Court explains H&C relief test requires exceptional misfortunes and weighing all relevant facts and factors.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy holds applicant need only show likely discrimination, which may be inferred from group membership.
propositions.quote: the Supreme Court of Canada held that the applicant only needs to show that it is likely that discrimination will occur, and that such a conclusion may be inferred

propositions.text: Discrimination can be inferred from membership in a discriminated group; direct evidence of personal targeting not required.
propositions.quote: discrimination can be inferred where an applicant shows that he or she is a member of a group that is discriminated against. Discrimination for the purpose of humanitarian and compassionate applications “could manifest in isolated incidents or permeate systemically”

propositions.text: Officer erred by requiring direct evidence of personal targeting, undermining humanitarian purpose of s.25(1).
propositions.quote: the Officer required Jeyakannan Kanthasamy to present direct evidence that he would face such a risk of discrimination if deported. This not only undermines the humanitarian purpose of s. 25(1)

propositions.text: Evidence of discrimination experienced by others sharing applicant’s identity is relevant and reasonable inferences can be drawn.
propositions.quote: Evidence of discrimination experienced by others who share the applicant’s identity is therefore clearly relevant under s. 25(1), whether or not the applicant has evidence of being personally targeted, and reasonable inferences can be drawn from those experiences.

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy holds discrimination likely can be inferred from group membership; direct personal evidence not required.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Shackleford and Kanthasamy that H&C relief should only be granted in exceptional circumstances to avoid becoming alternative immigration scheme.
propositions.quote: Respondent cited Shackleford v Canada ... relying on Kanthasamy ... in which the Court opined that an H&C application should only be granted in exceptional circumstances. Otherwise, section 25 would risk becoming the alternative immigration scheme

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues H&C relief should be granted only in exceptional circumstances to avoid misuse.

propositions.text: Applicant’s argument that Officer turned positive H&C establishment factors into negative ones should be sustained.
propositions.quote: the Applicant’s argument that the Officer turned positive H&C establishment factors into negative ones should be sustained.

propositions.text: Officer used Applicant’s resilience and work skills as reasons to conclude Applicant could re-establish in Sri Lanka, not as positive H&C factors.
propositions.quote: the Officer noted that the Applicant was “resilient” and had obtained “work skills in Canada that could be transferrable in Sri Lanka”. Instead of considering those factors as relevant to his H&C application, the Officer instead opined that this demonstrated that the Applicant could re-establish in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer unreasonably turned positive establishment factors into negative ones against Applicant.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer reasonably considered establishment factors independently and gave negative weight in context of immigration history.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer reasonably considered the establishment factors independently and gave it negative weight within the context of the Applicant’s past immigration history

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Respondent’s argument that Officer’s findings were reasonable.
propositions.quote: I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent defends Officer’s reasoning; Court disagrees and rejects that defense.

propositions.text: Officer cannot turn positive establishment factors into negative ones; such reasoning is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Officer is not allowed to turn positive establishment factors into negative ones

propositions.text: Singh case criticized use of positive establishment factors to deny H&C relief.
propositions.quote: This Court held in Singh ... The Officer’s analysis regarding the Applicants’ establishment in Canada was unreasonable because it turned positive factors that weigh in favour of granting an exemption into a justification for denying it.

propositions.text: Positive establishment factors cannot be used as a sword against applicants; this is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the officer cannot, as s/he does here, use the Applicants’ shield against them as a sword.

propositions.text: Use of positive establishment factors to attenuate future hardship is problematic and cautioned against in Lauture.
propositions.quote: the Officer committed this error by applauding the Applicants’ successful ability to assimilate to the Canadian milieu, but then using those positive skills to their detriment

paragraphs.summary: Court explains legal principle that positive establishment factors cannot be used negatively, citing Singh and Lauture.

propositions.text: Court agrees Officer unreasonably turned positive establishment factors into negative ones, making conclusion unintelligible.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that the Officer unreasonably turned positive establishment factors on their head. ... This conclusion is unintelligible

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees Officer’s reasoning turning positive factors negative is unintelligible and unreasonable.

propositions.text: Officers deciding PRRA and H&C applications simultaneously risk confusing distinct analyses and must keep processes separate.
propositions.quote: officers who rule on both types of applications at the same time are “at risk of confusing the two separate and distinct analyses required by these procedures… and may be drawn to the same conclusion [and therefore] extra care should be taken to ensure the two processes are kept separate.”

paragraphs.summary: Court states officers deciding PRRA and H&C applications simultaneously risk confusion and must keep analyses separate.

propositions.text: The Officer considered some evidence in PRRA but ignored some relevant evidence in H&C decision, contradicting their finding.
propositions.quote: the Officer considered some evidentiary elements in making their findings on the PRRA application, but then ignored some of the same relevant evidence in the H&C decision

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered evidence in PRRA but ignored contradictory relevant evidence in the H&C decision.

propositions.text: Omission to consider relevant contradictory evidence is unreasonable per Vavilov para 128.
propositions.quote: the omission to consider relevant objective evidence that is contradictory to the findings is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 128)

propositions.text: Decision maker cannot cherry-pick evidence but must explain why contradicting evidence is given little or no weight.
propositions.quote: The decision maker is not allowed to choose the evidence that fits its rationale, but ignore existing evidence that point to a contradictory conclusion

propositions.text: Decision maker must explain preference despite contradicting evidence (Ehigiator para 74; Rajput 2022 FC 65 para 25).
propositions.quote: the decision maker must explain why little or no weight had to be assigned to the contradicting evidence and why it preferred, in light of the contradicting evidence, to dismiss the application (Ehigiator at para 74; Rajput v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 65 at para 25)

paragraphs.summary: The court states the law that ignoring contradictory evidence is unreasonable and requires explanation, citing Vavilov, Ehigiator, and Rajput.

propositions.text: Applicant provided evidence of growing discrimination against Tamils in Sri Lanka, which Officer considered but ignored in H&C analysis.
propositions.quote: the Applicant provided documentary evidence showing that Tamils were facing growing discrimination in Sri Lanka today and that he was part of this group. The Officer considered that evidence, but failed to consider it entirely for the purposes of the H&C analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant showed evidence of Tamil discrimination, which the Officer considered but ignored in the H&C decision.

propositions.text: Officer considered discrimination evidence in PRRA but excluded it from H&C analysis, which was relevant and should have been considered.
propositions.quote: While that information was considered in the PRRA analysis, it was excluded from the H&C analysis. However, that information remained relevant and ought to have been considered and analyzed in the H&C decision

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider and analyze relevant evidence in H&C decision.
propositions.quote: The Officer failed to do so

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered discrimination evidence in PRRA but wrongly excluded it from H&C analysis, failing to consider relevant evidence.

propositions.text: Officer either failed to appreciate PRRA vs H&C differences or failed to weigh contradicting evidence; reasons lack explanation for ignoring important evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer either failed to appreciate the differences between the PRRA test and the H&C criteria, or failed to consider and weigh contradicting evidence. Either way, the reasons do not provide an explanation as to why that important evidence played no role in the Officer’s decision-making process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to appreciate test differences or weigh contradicting evidence, giving no explanation for ignoring important evidence.

propositions.text: Discrimination, harassment, or threats may not meet PRRA test but are important in H&C process.
propositions.quote: issues as to potential discrimination, harassment, or threats of criminal violence, even if they don’t meet the PRRA test, may directly impact the Applicant if he is removed. Those are important considerations in the H&C process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds discrimination and threats, even if not meeting PRRA test, are important in H&C considerations.

propositions.text: H&C test is broader than strict hardship, considering humanitarian and compassionate factors (Kim 2020 FC 581; Yanchak 2019 FC 117; Kanthasamy para 25).
propositions.quote: The correct legal test is not a strict hardships lens, but a broader one that considers the humanitarian and compassionate factors that is responsive to the facts of the case (Kanthasamy at para 25)

propositions.text: Officer erred by applying incorrect legal test in H&C decision.
propositions.quote: The Officer failed to do so, and thus erred by applying an incorrect legal test

paragraphs.summary: The court states the H&C test is broader and finds the Officer erred by applying an incorrect legal test.

propositions.text: Officer did not rely on most up-to-date evidence relevant to H&C assessment.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that for the H&C application, the Officer did not appear to rely on the most up-to-date evidence that was relevant to the H&C assessment

propositions.text: Sri Lanka's situation is fluid; Officer should have relied on recent objective evidence like UNHCR Guidelines.
propositions.quote: in the circumstances of this case where Sri Lanka is a country in which the situation is fluid, the Officer was able to and should have relied on the most recent objective evidence (more specifically the UNHCR Eligibility Guidelines)

propositions.text: PRRA should be based on up-to-date country condition evidence (Krishnapillai 2022 FC 485; Navaratnam 2018 FC 247; Rasalingam 2017 FC 718).
propositions.quote: To the extent reasonably possible, a PRRA should be based on up-to-date country condition evidence

propositions.text: Sri Lanka's political leadership changed in 2019, affecting conditions for Tamils.
propositions.quote: there is a new Prime Minister, Mahinda Rajapaksa and a new President, the Prime Minister’s brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa elected and appointed in 2019

propositions.text: Applicant lacked benefit of timely up-to-date PRRA assessment (Justice Favel in Navaratnam).
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied this Applicant had the benefit of a timely up-to-date PRRA assessment, as per Justice Favel in Navaratnam v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 247

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Applicant that Officer failed to use up-to-date evidence; cites cases requiring timely PRRA assessments given Sri Lanka's fluid situation.

propositions.text: Decision lacks intelligibility and is unreasonable; judicial review granted; matter remitted to different officer.
propositions.quote: the decision lacks intelligibility and is therefore not reasonable. JUDGMENT in IMM-9026-21 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: This application for judicial review is granted. The matter is remitted for redetermination by a different officer

propositions.text: No questions for certification arise or were argued.
propositions.quote: No questions for certification were argued, and I agree none arise

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the decision is unreasonable, grants judicial review, remits the matter, and finds no certification questions.
